observations.text: SP recognized the nose-low unusual attitude but, due to a delayed instrument transition to the attitude indicator, applied the wing-leveling and pitch inputs only after the IP directed the recovery sequence. The IP flew part of the initial correction, with the result that level flight was regained 500 feet below the entry altitude, beyond the 300 feet limit. Performance is at the desired standard for this training section but marginal; independent recognition of the attitude type and prompt self-initiated recovery are expected to improve over the next sorties.

SP correctly identified the nose-high unusual attitude and, with the IP's verbal prompts only, added power, lowered the nose toward the horizon on the attitude indicator and leveled the wings without further assistance. Recognition and correction were made with delay but were self-executed, with roll-out 10 degrees off the entry heading and level flight regained 300 feet from the entry altitude. No IP's intervention on the controls was required. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP identified the nose-low unusual attitude promptly, reduced power, leveled the wings on the attitude indicator and raised the nose to the level flight attitude without prompting. Minor errors in the rate of pitch recovery were recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, and level flight was regained 200 feet below the entry altitude with airspeed 15 KIAS high and heading within 8 degrees. The A/C was not flown into stall and no limitation was exceeded. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP recognized the nose-high unusual attitude immediately, added power, lowered the nose toward the horizon and leveled the wings using the control and performance instruments in the correct order. The recovery was accurate and rapid, with level flight regained within 100 feet of the entry altitude, airspeed within 8 KIAS and heading within 4 degrees, without IP's intervention. Instrument flight references were used IAW AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 throughout. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP recognized both the nose-high and the nose-low presentations at the first look at the attitude indicator and applied the correct recovery sequence with exceptional smoothness. Deviations at level-off were negligible, within 50 feet of altitude, 3 KIAS and 2 degrees of heading, and the loss of altitude in the nose-low recovery was the minimum available for the entry condition. No A/C limitation was approached and no IP's intervention was required at any point. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an incorrect recovery sequence in which nose-low pitch correction was applied before the wings were leveled, did not recover the A/C in level flight without exceeding its limitations, since G loading was applied at more than 90 degrees of bank. The IP intervened on the controls to unload and roll the A/C upright, with the result that the recovery finished 600 feet below the entry altitude and 35 KIAS above the entry airspeed. Review of the nose-low recovery sequence is required before the next instrument sortie.

SP, due to the startle effect at the onset of the unusual attitude, did not timely recognize the type of attitude presented and made no control input for several seconds. Power remained at the entry setting while the nose-low attitude developed, so the IP had to direct and then execute part of the recovery. Level flight was regained 550 feet low and 30 KIAS fast, beyond the 300 feet and 20 KIAS limits.

SP recognized the nose-high unusual attitude and completed the recovery, but the initial power addition and pitch reduction were applied only after the IP's verbal prompts. Errors were recognized and corrected with delay, with roll-out 10 degrees off the entry heading and level flight regained 300 feet low, at the limit of the desired standard. Performance meets the MIF for this training section but is marginal; more prompt self-initiated action on recognition is expected to improve.

SP recognized the type of unusual attitude without prompting and applied the recovery sequence in the correct order, leveling the wings before raising the nose from the nose-low attitude. Small errors in power management were recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, and level flight was regained 180 feet from the entry altitude with airspeed 14 KIAS high and heading within 7 degrees. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP recovered from both the nose-up and the nose-down presentations promptly and with the minimum loss of altitude for the entry condition, using the attitude indicator as the control instrument and cross-checking the performance instruments. Level flight was regained within 120 feet of altitude, 7 KIAS and 5 degrees of heading, with no approach to stall and no exceedance of A/C limitations. The recovery was accurate, rapid and completed without IP's intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP identified each unusual attitude at the first cross-check and flew the recovery with exceptional precision, sequencing power, bank and pitch without hesitation. Level flight was re-established with negligible deviations, inside 50 feet of altitude, 4 KIAS and 2 degrees of heading, and the altitude lost in the nose-low recovery was the minimum available. Instrument flight references were applied IAW AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 with no IP's intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a reversed recovery sequence in which back pressure was applied before the bank was reduced, did not recover the A/C in level flight without exceeding its limitations, with G loading applied at more than 90 degrees of bank. The IP intervened on the controls to unload and roll the A/C upright, and the recovery ended 700 feet below the entry altitude with airspeed 40 KIAS above the entry value. The priorities of the nose-low recovery require review before the next instrument sortie.

SP, due to unrecognized spatial disorientation in the absence of an external horizon, did not timely recognize the type of unusual attitude and made pitch inputs opposite to those required for the nose-high presentation. Airspeed decayed toward the stall while the bank increased unchecked, so the IP took control and executed the recovery. Level flight was regained 800 feet from the entry altitude, well beyond the 300 feet limit.

SP, due to chasing the performance instruments instead of first establishing the required attitude on the attitude indicator, did not apply the recovery inputs promptly, and the pitch and bank corrections were completed only after the IP's verbal prompts. Recognition and correction of the nose-low attitude were made with delay, with the result that level flight was regained 300 feet below the entry altitude, at the limit of the standard, with airspeed 20 KIAS high. No IP's intervention on the controls was required.

SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check that left the aircraft state unmonitored at the entry, recognized the nose-high unusual attitude with delay and did not add power until prompted verbally by the IP. The recovery was then completed unaided, but roll-out was 10 degrees off the entry heading and level flight was regained 300 feet low, at the limit of the desired standard. Timely recognition of the attitude type requires a continuous scan of the control and performance instruments.

SP recognized both unusual attitudes without prompting and recovered the A/C in level flight without approaching stall or exceeding A/C limitations. Minor over-control in pitch during the nose-low recovery was corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, leaving level flight 250 feet from the entry altitude with airspeed 18 KIAS high and heading 9 degrees off the entry value. Performance is within the desired standard but marginal for this training section; a smoother pitch capture and tighter altitude control are expected to improve with practice.

SP recognized the type of each unusual attitude at once and applied the correct sequence of power, bank and pitch, referencing the attitude indicator as the control instrument. Level flight was regained rapidly and accurately, within 110 feet of altitude, 6 KIAS and 4 degrees of heading, with the minimum loss of altitude in the nose-low presentation and without IP's intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP demonstrated exceptional accuracy in both recoveries, establishing the level flight attitude with a single smooth correction from each presentation. Deviations at level-off were negligible, within 40 feet of altitude, 3 KIAS and 2 degrees of heading, and airspeed approached neither the stall nor the maximum operating limit. Instrument flight references were used IAW AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 with no prompting of any kind. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to failure to reduce power at the entry to the nose-low unusual attitude, did not recover the A/C without approaching its airspeed limitation, and the pitch input was applied while the wings were still banked more than 60 degrees. The IP intervened on the controls to complete the recovery, with the result that level flight was regained 650 feet below the entry altitude and 45 KIAS above the entry airspeed. The power and bank priorities of the nose-low recovery require review.

SP, due to poor workload distribution, with aircraft control, radio communication and the recovery sequence attempted simultaneously, did not maintain the instrument cross-check and failed to recognize the nose-high attitude before airspeed decayed toward the stall. No corrective input was produced without assistance, so the IP directed and executed part of the recovery. The A/C finished 500 feet from the entry altitude and 30 degrees off the entry heading, beyond the limits of 300 feet and 10 degrees.

SP, due to a non-standardized instrument scan in which the attitude indicator was not used as the primary control reference, did not identify the nose-low unusual attitude promptly and applied the wing-leveling input only after the IP's verbal prompt. Recognition and correction were made with delay, although the recovery was completed without IP's intervention on the controls. Level flight was regained 300 feet low, with airspeed 20 KIAS high and heading 10 degrees off the entry value, at the limit of the standard.

SP, due to attention captured by a single engine indication while the aircraft state went unmonitored, did not recognize the developing nose-high unusual attitude and began the recovery only after the IP's verbal prompts. Power addition and pitch reduction were then applied correctly but late, with the result that the A/C decelerated to the onset of the stall warning before accelerating in the recovery. Level flight was regained 300 feet from the entry altitude and 10 degrees off heading, at the limit of the desired standard, without IP's intervention on the controls.

SP, due to an over-controlled pitch input during the nose-low recovery, momentarily raised the nose above the level flight attitude and did not capture the entry altitude in a single correction. The error was recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, and no A/C limitation was exceeded. Level flight was regained 220 feet below the entry altitude, with airspeed 16 KIAS high and heading within 8 degrees.

SP, due to a skill-based error in the roll input during the nose-high recovery, allowed the bank to increase before the wings were leveled and did not roll out on the entry heading in one correction. The deviation was recognized and self-corrected without IP's intervention, with the result that level flight was regained 190 feet from the entry altitude, with airspeed 13 KIAS low and heading 9 degrees off the entry value. The A/C was not flown into stall and no limitation was approached.

SP recognized the type of each unusual attitude without prompting and recovered the A/C to level flight rapidly, with the minimum loss of altitude and without IP's intervention. Level flight was re-established within 140 feet of altitude, 9 KIAS and 5 degrees of heading, at the outer edge of the desired standard, and the pitch capture in the nose-low recovery required two corrections. Performance meets the MIF for this training section but is marginal; a tighter first capture of the level flight attitude is expected to improve with repetition.

SP identified each unusual attitude on the first cross-check and flew both recoveries with exceptional precision, sequencing power, bank and pitch in one continuous and smooth correction. Deviations at level-off were negligible, inside 40 feet of altitude, 3 KIAS and 2 degrees of heading, and the altitude lost from the nose-low presentation was the minimum available for the entry condition. Control and performance instruments were used IAW AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 with no prompting and no IP's intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.
